extracted.intended_audience: regulated electric power industry (coal-fired steam EGUs), state permitting authorities, EPA rulemaking stakeholders and commenters
extracted.subtask_short: EPA BSER evaluation for coal EGUs
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations the EPA uses in determining the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for existing coal-fired steam electric generating units (EGUs), including cost-reasonableness, non-air quality impacts, permitting, and implementation requirements for CCS and alternative controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall cost reasonableness assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA considered the total annual costs of the rule as compared to past CAA rules for the electricity sector and as compared to the industry's annual revenues and annual capital expenditures, and considered the effects of this rule on electricity prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare total annualized program costs to historical CAA rules, industry revenues and capital expenditures, and projected electricity price impacts to judge whether costs are reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost metrics for assessing control cost reasonableness ($/MWh and $/ton CO2e)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA developed two metrics for assessing the cost reasonableness of controls: the increase in cost of electricity due to controls, measured in $/MWh, and the control costs of removing a ton of pollutant, measured in $/ton CO2e. The costs presented are in 2019 dollars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both $/MWh and $/ton CO2e as indicators; compare candidate control costs to these metrics rather than treating them as bright-line limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior-required control costs as benchmarks (FGD, SCR)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA compares control costs across technologies—steam generating units and combustion turbines—because costs of previously required controls (e.g., wet/dry FGD for SO2, SCR for NOx) are indicative of what is reasonable for the power sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmark proposed control costs against historically required controls where the agency has previously mandated and industry has complied (e.g., wet FGD annualized costs of $14.80–$18.50/MWh; SCR costs $10.60–$11.80/MWh).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrics are indicators, not bright-line standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA does not consider either of these metrics ($18.50/MWh and $98/ton CO2e) to be bright line standards that distinguish between levels of control costs that are reasonable and levels that are unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat quantitative benchmarks as useful indications of reasonableness; consider broader context and multiple lines of cost information rather than a strict cutoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to prior CCS cost estimates and tax incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA reevaluated CCS cost reasonableness in light of falling CCS costs (NETL reports: 2015 $74/MWh → 2022 $44/MWh incremental levelized costs) and increases in the IRC section 45Q tax credit (from $50 to $85/metric ton, with higher values for EOR/industrial uses) plus monetization options (direct pay and transferability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider updated technology cost reports and changed federal incentives (45Q) when assessing whether CCS qualifies as BSER; incorporate both cost declines and credit monetization into cost-reasonableness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of non-air quality health and environmental impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considered non-GHG emissions impacts, water use impacts, the transport and sequestration of captured CO2, and energy requirements resulting from CCS for steam generating units, and finds protections in place to mitigate localized adverse consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate potential localized non-GHG harms (HAPs, VOCs, water, sequestration risks) and whether existing permitting, monitoring, and regulatory frameworks mitigate those risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy requirements and energy penalty assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: For a steam generating unit with 90 percent amine-based CO2 capture, parasitic/auxiliary energy demand increases and net power output decreases (e.g., a ~474 MW-net unit could drop to ~425 MW-net with CCS; net efficiency reduction ~23%). Auxiliary cogeneration may be used but is part of the 'designated facility' so its CO2 emissions are subject to the standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify capacity and efficiency impacts, account for auxiliary equipment as part of the facility for compliance, and weigh energy penalties against GHG reduction benefits; EPA considers the energy penalty 'not unreasonable' relative to benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of co-pollutant emissions (SO2, PM, NOx) and required mitigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Amine-based CO2 capture can increase emissions of SO2, PM, and NOx; EPA expects flue gas conditioning and control equipment (FGD, polishing quencher, WESP, PM control upgrades) and NSR permitting to mitigate and review such co-pollutant increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate need for additional flue gas conditioning/controls; include associated costs in BSER cost analyses; use NSR as backstop to review and require additional mitigation where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: NOx limits to avoid solvent degradation and nitrosamine formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Limits on NOx levels of the flue gas to avoid solvent degradation and nitrosamine formation vary; existing combustion controls may suffice for most units but some units may need to install SCR. Increased utilization could trigger major NSR requiring SCR or other requirements depending on permitting outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate solvent sensitivity to NOx, consider SCR installation and NSR permitting thresholds, and permit authorities may use minor/major NSR pathways or state plan enforceable limits to address NOx increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA guidance and NSR/BACT consideration for co-pollutant increases
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA plans to review and update guidance on NSR permitting, specifically with respect to BACT determinations for GHG emissions and consideration of co-pollutant increases from sources installing CCS; costs of anticipated co-pollutant controls are included in IPM modeling and BSER cost calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting authorities and stakeholders should expect updated EPA guidance; analyses should include co-pollutant control costs and potential permitting outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazardous air pollutant (HAP) and VOC control expectations for amine-based systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Solvent degradation can produce HAPs and VOCs; water/acid washes and demisters are effective at removing gaseous amine and amine degradation products, but aldehyde control may require separate systems and some mitigation technologies are still under development. Case-by-case MACT (CAA section 112(g)) may apply if a carbon capture system is a major source of listed HAPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess solvent-specific emissions, plan for water/acid wash and demister controls, consider separate aldehyde controls where necessary, and evaluate potential applicability of section 112(g) MACT analyses for listed HAPs (e.g., nitrosamines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and monitoring limitations for nitrosamines
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement of nitrosamine emissions may be challenging when the concentration is low (e.g., less than 1 part per billion, dry basis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize analytical detection limits when setting permit limits and designing monitoring/measurement strategies; permits may rely on post-startup testing to set formal limits where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of air toxics permitting and risk assessment (Project Tundra example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Project Tundra permit included PTE values for listed HAPs and an air toxics assessment showing total maximum individual carcinogenic risk of ~1.02E-6 (below ND-DEQ threshold of 1E-5) and hazard index 0.022 (below threshold of 1), with formaldehyde and nitrosamine species as key drivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use facility-specific PTE and risk assessments to set permit limits; results will depend on emissions, controls, stack parameters, ambient conditions, and nearby populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationary source aggregation criteria for permitting
rubrics_metrics.description: To permit a CO2 capture plant as a separate entity, the source must demonstrate that the EGU and CO2 capture plant are not a single stationary source under NSR. NSR criteria require aggregation if activities (1) belong to the same industrial grouping (SIC), (2) are on contiguous/adjacent properties, and (3) are under common control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting determinations will consider SIC codes, property adjacency, and common control; EPA expects most collocated EGU and capture plants to be aggregated as a single stationary source given integrated operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water use and cooling system design considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Water consumption increases with carbon capture (e.g., up to 36% gross increase) due to solvent makeup and cooling demand; cooling system design (e.g., relying on condensed flue gas water, dry/hybrid cooling) affects external water consumption and applicability in water-limited regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess site-specific cooling design options (wet, dry, hybrid) and regional water availability; treat water-use requirements as manageable but design-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 capture plant siting and land-use footprint
rubrics_metrics.description: CO2 capture systems have a sizeable physical footprint. EPA reviewed analyses showing most large coal-fired units have adjacent land available and concluded siting/land-use requirements are not unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate land availability (on-site or adjacent) and potential need for longer duct runs; EPA expects siting constraints will not generally preclude CCS deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport and geologic sequestration protections and frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA oversight of supercritical CO2 pipeline safety, UIC Class VI and II regulations under the SDWA, and GHGRP subparts RR and VV provide protections to address transport and sequestration risks; these regulatory frameworks inform the conclusion that CCS can be BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure project plans align with PHMSA pipeline safety standards, appropriate UIC permitting, and GHGRP reporting requirements; rely on these frameworks to manage transportation and storage risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy-sector reliability and long-term structural impact analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considered nationwide and long-term impacts on the power sector and concluded designating CCS as BSER for long-term units would have limited and non-adverse impacts on sector structure or reliability, given projected deployment timelines and compliance deadlines (e.g., Jan 1, 2032).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze grid reliability, resource planning timelines, likely deployment rates, and the reasonableness of generation cost increases when assessing BSER impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of CO2 emissions reductions achievable with CCS
rubrics_metrics.description: CCS can reduce the mass of CO2 emissions by 90 percent or more at the source; 90 percent capture corresponds to ~88.4% lower lb CO2/MWh-gross (and ~87.1% lb/MWh-net) compared to units without capture (NETL retrofit findings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capture-percentage and lb/MWh reductions together to characterize performance; consider the incentive effects (e.g., 45Q) that may increase utilization but are outweighed by emission-rate reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of technology development through BSER designation
rubrics_metrics.description: Designating CCS as BSER is expected to provide for meaningful advancement of CCS technology by prompting deployment (EPA IPM modeling indicates additional GW and TWh generation with CCS under the rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider technology advancement and cross-sector spillovers as a factor in BSER decisions; quantify anticipated deployment benefits where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to earlier NSPS determinations (2015 NSPS) driven by historical costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2015 NSPS determined BSER for newly constructed coal-fired EGUs based on CCS with 16–23% capture because costs were higher at that time; current lower costs and 45Q change the analysis for existing sources even if the 2015 NSPS is retained pending evidence of new coal-fired construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for temporal changes in technology costs and incentives when comparing to prior NSPS determinations; updating new-source standards may not be prioritized absent evidence of new builds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to transfer or report captured CO2 under GHGRP (40 CFR part 98 subparts)
rubrics_metrics.description: EGUs that capture CO2 to meet the emission standard must report under GHGRP requirements in 40 CFR part 98 (including subpart PP). If injection occurs onsite, report under subpart RR or VV; if injected offsite, EGUs must transfer captured CO2 to an entity that reports under subpart RR or VV (or to a facility with an EPA innovative technology waiver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure chain-of-custody and reporting arrangements are in place for captured CO2; verify receiving facilities report under appropriate GHGRP subparts or have waivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why partial-capture CCS was not selected as BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial capture CCS was not determined to be BSER because emission reductions are lower and costs would, in general, be higher; designs for 90% capture take greater advantage of economies of scale, and 45Q incentives favor higher capture amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer higher capture designs that benefit from economies of scale and maximize incentives; assess both absolute emission reductions and cost-effectiveness when rejecting partial-capture options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of natural gas co-firing as an alternative (40% co-firing)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA determined 40 percent natural gas co-firing to qualify as the BSER for the medium-term subcategory (units that will cease operation by Jan 1, 2039). For long-term units, although co-firing is demonstrated and has reasonable energy/non-air impacts, variable costs are higher such that total $/ton costs are generally higher and thus it was not selected as BSER for long-term units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating co-firing, compare capital and variable costs to CCS on both $/MWh and $/ton bases, and consider subcategory-specific retirement timelines and cost structures.
